lessons.title: if, else and comparisons
lessons.summary: Making a program choose between two paths.
lessons.notes:
**Selection** means the program picks which lines to run.

```python
if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")
else:
    print("Child")
```

Comparison operators: `==` equal to, `!=` not equal to, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`.

Two classic mistakes:
- using `=` (assignment) when you mean `==` (comparison)
- forgetting the colon or the indentation under the `if`
lessons.worked_example_note: Only one of the two `print` lines can ever run. The indented block belongs to the branch above it.

lessons.title: elif chains and logical operators
lessons.summary: More than two options, and conditions joined with and/or/not.
lessons.notes:
Use `elif` for a chain of options. Python checks them in order and stops at the first one that is true, so **order matters** — put the strictest boundary first.

```python
if mark >= 80:
    grade = "9"
elif mark >= 60:
    grade = "7"
else:
    grade = "4"
```

Join conditions with `and` (both must be true), `or` (at least one), `not` (reverses it).

OCR wording tip: *"between 10 and 20 inclusive"* becomes `if 10 <= n <= 20:` or `if n >= 10 and n <= 20:`.
lessons.worked_example_note: `and` needs both sides to be true. Compare strings with `==` and remember they are case sensitive.

lessons.title: Exam-style selection problems
lessons.summary: Working out the boundaries from a written scenario.
lessons.notes:
Exam scenarios hide the conditions inside sentences. Build a small table before you code:

```text
Condition          Output
90 or more         Gold
70 to 89           Silver
less than 70       Bronze
```

Then write one branch per row, strictest first. Check the **boundary values** (exactly 90, exactly 70) — that is where marks are usually lost.
lessons.worked_example:
# Discount: 10% off orders of 50 or more, 5% off orders of 20 or more
total = float(input())
if total >= 50:
    total = total * 0.9
elif total >= 20:
    total = total * 0.95
print(round(total, 2))
lessons.worked_example_note: There is no `else` here because orders under £20 need no change at all.

tasks.title: Positive or negative
tasks.brief: Read a whole number. Print `Positive` if it is greater than 0. Otherwise print `Not positive`.
hints: Exactly one of the two branches runs — decide the condition first, then fill in what each branch prints.
if n > 0: print("Positive") else: print("Not positive")

tasks.title: Old enough to vote
tasks.brief: Read an age. Print `Can vote` if the age is 18 or more. Otherwise print `Too young`.
hints: "18 or more" includes exactly 18, so use >= rather than >.
if age >= 18: print("Can vote") else: print("Too young")

tasks.title: Bigger of two
tasks.brief: Read two whole numbers, one per line. Print the larger one. If they are equal, print `Equal` instead.
hints: There are three possible outcomes here, not two — you need a third branch for the equal case.
if a > b: print(a), elif b > a: print(b), else: print("Equal")

tasks.title: Largest of three
tasks.brief:
Read three whole numbers, one per line. Print the largest of the three. If two or more of them are tied for the largest, print `Tie` instead.

For example, 3, 9 and 5 prints 9. 7, 7 and 2 prints Tie.
hints: Python's built-in max() finds the largest of several values for you: max(a, b, c). Once you have it, count how many of a, b and c equal it.
largest = max(a, b, c), count = (a == largest) + (b == largest) + (c == largest), then print("Tie") if count > 1 else print(largest)

tasks.title: Traffic light
tasks.brief: A program reads the colour of a traffic light. Print `Stop` for `red`, `Get ready` for `amber` and `Go` for `green`. For anything else, print `Broken`.
hints: You have four possible outputs, so you need an if / elif / elif / else chain, not just if / else.
String comparisons are case sensitive — "red" and "Red" are not equal

tasks.title: In range
tasks.brief: Read a whole number. Print `In range` if it is between 10 and 20 inclusive — meaning 10 and 20 themselves both count as in range. Otherwise print `Out of range`.
hints: Python lets you chain two comparisons in one condition: 10 <= n <= 20 is true exactly when n is between 10 and 20, inclusive.
if 10 <= n <= 20: print("In range") else: print("Out of range")

tasks.title: Login with two checks
tasks.brief: Read a username, then a password, one per line. Print `Welcome` only if the username is exactly `admin` and the password is exactly `hcode`. Otherwise print `Rejected`.
hints: Both checks must be true at once, so join the two conditions with and.
if username == "admin" and password == "hcode": print("Welcome") else: print("Rejected")

tasks.title: VIP eligibility
tasks.brief:
A loyalty scheme grants VIP status under either of two rules:

- the customer is 18 or older AND has been a member for at least 2 years, OR
- the customer has been a member for at least 5 years, whatever their age

Read the customer's age, then the number of years they've been a member, one per line. Print `VIP` if either rule applies, otherwise print `Not VIP`.

For example, age 20 with 3 years membership is VIP (meets the first rule). Age 16 with 6 years membership is also VIP (meets the second rule — age doesn't matter there).
hints: Write the two rules as two separate conditions first, then join them with or: (age >= 18 and years >= 2) or years >= 5.
age = int(input()), years = int(input()), if (age >= 18 and years >= 2) or years >= 5: print("VIP") else: print("Not VIP")

tasks.title: Swimming pool entry
tasks.brief:
A swimming pool charges different prices by age:

- under 5: free
- 5 to 15: £2
- 16 to 64 (adult): £4
- 65 or over: £2

Read a person's age. Display the price they pay, as a whole number of pounds.

For example, age 30 pays £4, so print `4`.
hints: Build the branches in age order, from youngest to oldest, checking the strictest boundary first. There are four price groups, not two, so you'll need an elif chain.
if age < 5: price = 0, elif age < 16: price = 2, elif age < 65: price = 4, else: price = 2 — the last two branches both give 2, they're just different age groups

tasks.title: Parcel size checker
tasks.brief:
A courier classifies parcels by weight in kilograms:

- up to and including 2 kg: `Small`
- over 2 kg, up to and including 10 kg: `Medium`
- over 10 kg, up to and including 30 kg: `Large`
- over 30 kg: `Refused`

Read the weight as a decimal. Display the classification.
hints: Check the Refused case and the Large case before the smaller ones, so the boundaries at exactly 2, 10 and 30 land in the right group.
if weight > 30: print("Refused"), elif weight > 10: print("Large"), elif weight > 2: print("Medium"), else: print("Small")

tasks.title: Quiz feedback
tasks.brief:
A quiz is marked out of 20:

- 18 or more: `Excellent`
- 14 to 17: `Good`
- 10 to 13: `Pass`
- below 10: `Revise this topic`

A mark outside the range 0 to 20 is invalid and should display `Invalid mark` instead of any of the above.

Read the mark scored. Display the appropriate result.
hints: Check whether the mark is invalid (below 0 or above 20) before checking any of the grade boundaries.
Order the grade boundaries from highest down, same pattern as the lesson's elif example

tasks.title: Theme park ride restrictions
tasks.brief:
A theme park needs software to check whether a visitor may ride a rollercoaster.

- A visitor may ride if they are at least 140 cm tall AND aged 12 or over.
- A visitor who is tall enough (140 cm or more) but under 12 may still ride if an adult is with them.
- Anyone under 140 cm may never ride, whatever their age or whether an adult is with them.

Read three lines of input: height in centimetres (whole number), age (whole number), then `yes` or `no` for whether an adult is with them.

Output exactly one of:
- `Ride allowed`
- `Ride allowed with adult`
- `Ride refused`
hints: Deal with the height rule first — anyone under 140 cm is refused no matter what the other answers are.
Then, among those tall enough, split on age, then on the adult answer

tasks.title: Broadband billing
tasks.brief:
An internet provider bills customers monthly:

- The standard package costs £25 per month and includes 100 GB of data.
- Data used above the 100 GB allowance costs £1.50 per whole gigabyte over the limit.
- Customers who have been with the provider for 24 months or more get a 10% discount on the whole bill, applied after any excess data charge has been added.

Read the gigabytes used (a whole number), then the number of months the customer has been with the provider (a whole number). Output the final bill, rounded to 2 decimal places, in the format `Bill: £<amount>`.

For example, 80 GB used over 5 months (no excess, no discount) gives `Bill: £25.0`.
hints: Excess data only applies when usage is above 100 — work that out first and add it to the base £25.
Apply the loyalty discount last, to the total bill so far, not just to the excess charge

tasks.title: Library fine system
tasks.brief:
A school library charges fines for late books:

- returned up to 3 days late: no fine
- from day 4 onwards: 20p per day late, counting all the days late, not just the days after day 3
- the fine is capped at £5.00, however late the book is
- students in Year 7 are never fined, whatever the rules above say

Read the number of days late (a whole number), then the student's year group (a whole number). Output the fine, in pounds, to 2 decimal places, in the format `Fine: £<amount>`.
hints: Check the Year 7 rule first — it overrides every other rule, so it should be the very first thing you check.
Work out the uncapped fine, then cap it: if fine > 5: fine = 5

tasks.title: Exam retake eligibility
tasks.brief:
An exam board decides whether a student may retake an exam:

- if the mark is 40 or above, the student has passed and does not need a retake, however many attempts they've had
- if the mark is below 40, the student may retake the exam if they have had fewer than 3 previous attempts
- if the mark is below 40 and they have already had 3 or more attempts, no more retakes are allowed

Read the mark (whole number), then the number of previous attempts (whole number). Print exactly one of `Passed`, `Retake allowed` or `No more attempts`.
hints: Check the pass condition first — if it's true, the number of attempts doesn't matter at all, so nothing else needs checking.
if mark >= 40: print("Passed"), elif attempts < 3: print("Retake allowed"), else: print("No more attempts")
